Institutional or university rankings attract a great deal of attention in academic policy circles and amongst the general public because they provide a clear comparison of academic institutions on a global scale. They serve various stakeholder groups, such as policy-makers, university managers and prospective students, acting, amongst other things, as a tool for strategic decision-making, for illustrating institutional excellence, or for choosing a place to study [@Waltman2012;@Johnes2018]. The methodology on which the rankings are based is sometimes subject to numerous criticisms, for example because of the tendency to summarise multiple dimensions of academic institutions’ performance into a single, often untransparent score [@vanRaan2005;@Piro2016;@Diprose2023]. This makes it difficult not only to interpret the results, but also fails to take sufficient account of the different missions and priorities of the institutions [@Waltman2012;@Huang2020].

In recent years, the inclusion of open access metrics in university rankings has gained in importance. Open access refers to free and unrestricted online access to research results [@Suber2012] and has become an important indicator of an academic institution’s commitment to open and transparent scientific practice. This trend is further supported by the requirements of funding organizations, which are increasingly viewing open access publishing as a condition for research funding [@Wellcome_Trust;@NIH;@DFG;@Fournier2017;@Huang2020a;@Ruecknagel2021]. In addition to the many institutions' own commitment to open access, these requirements provide a further incentive to make research findings available via open access. The inclusion of open access indicators in university rankings makes it possible to assess institutions’ open access activities and provides an additional dimension for comparison [@Diprose2023].

Following the argument of @Moed2016, it is assumed that a comparative analysis of several ranking systems can help users better understand, interpret, and use the information provided by these systems. This also applies to the open access dimension of rankings. When rankings are used to compare institutional open access engagement or to monitor corresponding activities, the informative value of ranking results depends substantially on how strongly the underlying ranking methodologies differ. To date, however, no systematic investigation appears to exist that specifically compares the open access dimension across several ranking systems.

In this study, institutional rankings with open access indicators were identified via a web search. Rankings were included if they met three criteria: (1) they constitute an institutional-level ranking (as opposed to, e.g., journal- or researcher-level rankings), (2) they include at least one open access indicator, and (3) they have a global geographic scope. Based on these criteria, five institutional rankings with open access as a comparative dimension could be identified: the Leiden Ranking 2025 (LR), the Leiden Ranking Open Edition 2025 (LROE), the SCImago Institutions Ranking 2025 (SIR), the Quacquarelli Symonds World University Rankings: Sustainability 2025 (QS), and the COKI OA Dashboard 2025 (COKI). All five rankings contain one or more open access indicators and are globally oriented in terms of their geographic coverage.

This page provides an overview of the characteristics of the five ranking systems, as well as an analysis of the extent to which the ranking results are comparable with one another. This includes, amongst other things, a comparison of the data sources and open-access indicators used by the rankings, as well as an assessment of the extent to which institutions can participate in the data collection carried out by the ranking providers. The focus here is particularly on the open access dimension.


## Institutional Rankings with Open Access as a Comparative Dimension

The following sections begin with a description of the core characteristics of the selected rankings. At the end of each section, details of the rankings are summarised in a drop-down text box headed ‘Ranking Details’. This includes, in particular, a comprehensive list of the open access indicators used in each ranking system.


### Leiden Ranking

The Leiden Ranking has been produced annually since 2007 by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) at Leiden University in the Netherlands [@Waltman2012;@LR_updates]. The ranking does not provide a traditional league table based on a single overall score, but rather presents various bibliometric indicators across the dimensions of *scientific impact*, *collaboration*, *Open Access* and *gender*. Indicators are presented in both size-dependent (absolute numbers) and size-independent (relative shares) form to account for differences in university size. The ranking also provides trend analyses over time and stability intervals to reflect statistical uncertainties [@LR_indicators;@LR_method]. 

The 2025 edition of the Leiden Ranking includes bibliometric data for 1,594 universities worldwide [@LR_method]. Indicators are reported for four-year periods; the 2025 edition extends these to include the period 2020--2023 [@LR_method]. Bibliographic data is retrieved from the Web of Science, however, only articles and reviews published in international scientific journals are taken into account [@LR_method]. Universities are selected on the basis of their research output, and must have at least 800 so-called *core publications* to be included in the ranking. *Core publications* are defined as publications that have appeared in international scientific journals in fields suitable for citation analysis. These publications must be written in English, have at least one author, must not have been retracted, and must have appeared in a so-called *core journal*. *Core journals* are defined through their international focus and must be situated in a field suitable for citation analysis. The Leiden Ranking does not use data provided directly by universities [@LR_method;@LR_universities].

A key characteristic of the Leiden Ranking is its focus on open access publications. Indicators relating to open access publishing were added in the 2019 edition of the ranking [@LR_updates]. To determine the open access status of publications, the Leiden Ranking uses OpenAlex as its data source [@LR_method;@LR_general].


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### Leiden Ranking Open Edition

The Leiden Ranking Open Edition has been compiled annually since 2024 [@LROE2024] by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS) at Leiden University in the Netherlands [@LROE_updates]. It is a near reproduction of the traditional Leiden Ranking using open data sources [@LROE2024] and, like the traditional ranking, does not provide a conventional league table, but rather various bibliometric indicators across the dimensions of *scientific impact*, *collaboration* and *Open Access*. In the Open Edition, the indicators are also presented in both size-dependent (absolute figures) and size-independent (relative shares) form to account for differences in the size of universities. Additionally, the Open Edition of the Leiden Ranking also provides trend analyses over time and stability intervals to address statistical uncertainties [@LROE_indicators]. 

The 2025 edition of the Leiden Ranking Open Edition introduces two changes compared to the 2024 edition: Firstly, in addition to *core publications*, so-called *non-core publications* are included in the preparation of the ranking. Secondly, unlike the 2024 edition and the traditional Leiden Ranking, bibliometric data from a larger number of universities is included [@vanEck2025c]. Whereas the 2024 version comprised bibliometric data for 1,506 universities worldwide [@LROE24_method], the 2025 version is based on bibliometric data from 2,831 universities [@LROE_universities; @vanEck2025c]. Indicators are reported for four-year periods; the 2025 version extends these to include the period 2020–2023 [@LROE_indicators]. Bibliographic data are retrieved from OpenAlex, and the respective indicators are calculated and reported separately for the set of *core publications* and for the combined set of *core publications* and *non-core publications*. The definition of *core publications* and *core journals* in the Leiden Ranking Open Edition is largely identical to that in the traditional Leiden Ranking [@LR_indicators;@LROE_indicators]. However, the Open Edition expands the set of *core publications* to include book chapters published in book series. Furthermore, all publications must contain not only author details but also affiliation details and references in order to be counted as *core publications* [@LROE_indicators]. Less restrictive criteria apply to *non-core publications*; for example, the restriction to English-language publications does not apply, and *non-core publications* may also have been published outside *core journals*, such as in journals with a national or regional focus, books, book series, or conference proceedings [@LROE_indicators].

The Leiden Ranking Open Edition also focuses on open access publications and offers largely the same open access indicators as the traditional Leiden Ranking, with the exception of the indicators relating to publications with an unclear open access status [@LROE_indicators]. Furthermore, a distinctive feature of the Leiden Ranking Open Edition is that the publications underlying the indicators can be viewed via the web interface [@LROE2024a].


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### SCImago Institutions Ranking

The SCImago Institutions Ranking has been compiled annually by the SCImago Research Group since 2009 [@Rousseau2018]. The ranking provides a traditional league table of academic and research-oriented institutions based on a composite indicator on a scale of 0 to 100. The composite indicator combines assessments across three dimensions: research, innovation and societal impact. The composite indicator is derived from a weighted combination of metrics across these dimensions, using both size-dependent and size-independent indicators. For each institution, the ranking also provides a series of charts, for example showing changes in ranking over time, comparisons at national, regional or global level, or similar institutions based on their publication profile [@SIR_method].

The 2025 version of the SCImago Institutions Ranking includes data for 9,755 institutions worldwide [@SIR]. The composite indicator is reported on an annual basis for a five-year period ending two years prior to the publication of the ranking; for the 2025 edition, this covers the period 2019--2023. Bibliographic data are retrieved from Scopus. Institutions are selected based on their publication output. In the final year of the period under review, institutions must have published at least 100 publications indexed in Scopus in order to be included in the ranking. Furthermore, at least 75% of an institution’s total publication output must consist of so-called *citable items*. For the SCImago Institutions Ranking, document types counted as *citable items* include articles, books, book chapters, conference papers, data papers, editorials, letters, notes, reviews and short surveys. [@SIR_method;@elsevier2026scopus].

Within the research dimension, which accounts for 50% of the composite indicator, an open access indicator was added to the ranking in the 2019 version. With a weighting of 2% within the research dimension, this indicator measures the percentage of documents published in open access journals or indexed in Unpaywall. To determine the open access status of publications, the SCImago Institutions Ranking uses Unpaywall as its data source [@SIR_method].


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### QS World University Rankings: Sustainability 

The QS World University Rankings: Sustainability has been compiled annually by Quacquarelli Symonds since 2023, following the publication of a pilot version in 2022 [@QS_date]. The ranking provides a traditional league table of higher education institutions based on a composite indicator for both the individual categories and sub-categories (*Lenses*), as well as an overall score. The category scores are displayed for all institutions assessed, whereas the overall scores are only shown up to a certain point and are then hidden [@QS_scores]. The QS World University Rankings: Sustainability assesses institutions across three dimensions: *Environmental Impact*, *Social Impact* and *Governance*.

The 2025 edition of the QS World University Rankings: Sustainability includes data on 1,744 higher education institutions worldwide [@QS_date]. Bibliographic data are retrieved from Scopus and cover a 5-year period [@QS_papers]. Only the following document types are taken into account: article, review, conference paper, book, book chapter, article in press, business article, data paper and report [@QS_paperdef;@QS_scopus]. Institutions are only included in the QS World University Rankings: Sustainability if, on the one hand, they meet the eligibility criteria for inclusion in at least one of the *QS World University Rankings*, *QS Rankings by Region* or *QS Rankings by Subject*, and, on the other hand, they achieve a non-zero score for specific indicators within the *Environmental Impact* and *Social Impact* dimensions. [@QS_sustain].

Within the *Governance* dimension, which accounts for 10% of the total score, one indicator relates to open access publications. This indicator is weighted at 1% within the *Governance* dimension and measures the share of open access publications in the total publication volume. This proportion is calculated separately for each of the six fields considered and aggregated into a weighted total. Gold and hybrid publications are given greater weight in the calculation than publications published via the green open access route. To determine the open access status of publications, the QS World University Rankings: Sustainability uses Unpaywall as its data source [@QS_governance].


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

### COKI OA Dashboard

The COKI Open Access Dashboard has been produced by the Curtin Open Knowledge Initiative since 2022 [@COKI_date; @COKI_newsletter]. The dashboard is not a traditional ranking, but institutions and countries can be sorted by their proportion of open access publications, as well as by their total and open access publication volumes [@COKI_date]. The dashboard also shows, for each country and institution, the platform through which open access publications are made available, both as an aggregate figure covering the entire publication period and broken down by individual publication years [@COKI_date].

The 18 August 2025 version of the COKI Open Access Dashboard includes data for 227 countries and 56,187 institutions worldwide [@COKI_how]. Bibliographic data is retrieved from several open data sources and covers the publication period 2000--2024; Crossref is used in particular to identify publications [@COKI_how;@COKI_dashboard]. The selection of document types is less restrictive than in the other ranking systems; the only exclusions are publications classified as datasets, databases, components, report components, peer reviews, funding awards, conference proceedings, journal issues, report series, book catalogues, and all publications without a specified document type. [@COKI_how]. Institutions must have at least 50 publications to be included in the COKI Open Access Dashboard, unless they were already included in the dataset when it was still based on Microsoft Academic Graph [@COKI_how].

The COKI Open Access Dashboard focuses exclusively on the open access activities of institutions and countries. Whereas the list view primarily displays the absolute number and the percentage of open access publications, detailed views of individual institutions and countries provide more nuanced breakdowns of publication activities and locations, supplemented by visualisations [@COKI_dashboard]. To determine the open access status of publications, the COKI Open Access Dashboard uses Unpaywall as its data source [@COKI_how].


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Comparability of Ranking Results

In order to assess how comparable the results of the selected rankings are, the subsequent sections focus on examining the following aspects: the number and overlap of institutions featured in all rankings, the geographical distribution of institutions across countries and regions of the world, the data sources used by the ranking systems, the open access indicators used by the rankings and their weighting, and the extent to which institutions can participate in the data collection process carried out by the ranking providers.

The aim is to examine the extent to which the individual ranking systems differ and what implications this may have for the use of a particular ranking in open access monitoring activities or strategic decision-making.

### Institutional Overlap

```{r}
#| label: loading-data
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(here)
library(tidyverse)
options(scipen = 999)

institutions_df_de_sector <- read_csv(here("rankings_notebook/data","institutions_df_de_sector.csv"))
institutions_df_de_univs <- read_csv(here("rankings_notebook/data", "institutions_df_de_univs.csv"))
pref_df <- read_csv(here("rankings_notebook/data", "pref_df.csv"))
qs_upset_merged <- read_csv(here("rankings_notebook/data","qs_upset_merged.csv"))
sir_upset_merged <- read_csv(here("rankings_notebook/data","sir_upset_merged.csv"))
```


To determine the institutional overlap between the rankings, first available ranking data was downloaded[^1]. In addition to the names and locations (country details, and in some cases details of regions and sub-regions) of all institutions, data from both versions of the Leiden Ranking and from the COKI OA Dashboard included identifiers from the [Research Organisation Registry (ROR)](https://ror.org/). Furthermore, data from the COKI OA Dashboard and the SCImago Institutions Ranking included sector classifications for all institutions represented in the rankings.

In order to uniquely match identical institutions across rankings using their ROR IDs, the data of the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking first had to be supplemented with ROR IDs. For this purpose, the complete ROR dataset in version 2.9 [@ror_data] was downloaded. Subsequently, an automated matching based on institutional name and country information was performed against the ROR data for both rankings. The QS data contained entries for a total of 1,743 institutions[^2], of which `r format(sum(is.na(qs_upset_merged$id)), big.mark=",", decimal.mark = ".")` institutions could not be assigned ROR IDs via the automated matching procedure.

It proved even more difficult to map ROR IDs to the 9,755 institutions included in the SCImago Institutions Ranking[^3]. Based on the automated matching process using the institutional name and country details, no ROR IDs could be assigned to `r format(sum(is.na(sir_upset_merged$id)), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions. This may be partly due to the fact that the SCImago Institutions Ranking also lists institutions that are classified as multinational [@SIR_method]. This appears to affect, in particular, companies that operate on a supra-regional level, such as [Google](https://www.scimagoir.com/institution.php?idp=89900). Although ROR also provides IDs for companies (see [Google](https://ror.org/00njsd438)), these appear to be assigned to specific countries. However, the greater difficulty for automated matching is likely to be the differences in naming conventions between the SCImago Institutions Ranking and ROR[^4]. To increase coverage with ROR IDs for the SCImago Institutions Ranking, a fuzzy matching approach was tested, which also took into account alternative name forms and acronyms from the ROR dataset. However, the result was not sufficiently accurate and would have required a significant amount of data cleaning. Overall, this represents a significant limitation on the usability of the SCImago dataset for a global analysis of institutional overlap.

Due to the limitations in assigning ROR IDs, it was decided to restrict the analysis of institutional overlap to German institutions. In the QS Sustainability Ranking dataset, a total of 50 institutions from Germany were identified, all of which could be assigned a ROR ID, either via automated matching or manual additions. In the SCImago Institutions Ranking dataset, a total of 364 German institutions were identified, of which 342 could not be assigned a ROR ID via automated matching. A manual assignment was carried out for these 342, however, no ROR ID could be assigned to 5 of these institutions as they have no record in ROR. Consequently, 385 institutions were included in the analysis of institutional overlap among German institutions for the SCImago Institutions Ranking.

@fig-2 quantifies the institutional overlap between German institutions across the various ranking systems. The figure only includes those institutions to which ROR IDs could be assigned.

![Institutional overlap for all German institutions with ROR IDs across five ranking systems](plots/all_de_institution_upset.png){#fig-2 group="upset"}

In total, after matching the ROR IDs `r format(n_distinct(institutions_df_de_sector$ror), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` unique institutions from Germany were identified across all ranking systems. As can be seen from @fig-2, the COKI OA Dashboard covers significantly more German institutions than all other ranking systems, both in total (`r format(sum(institutions_df_de_sector$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions, `r format(round(sum(institutions_df_de_sector$coki) / n_distinct(institutions_df_de_sector$ror) *100, 2), decimal.mark=".")`%), as well as in terms of the number of institutions not included in any other ranking system (`r format(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_sector, coki == 1 & lr == 0 & lroe == 0 & qs == 0 & sir == 0)$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions, `r format(round(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_sector, coki == 1 & lr == 0 & lroe == 0 & qs == 0 & sir == 0)$coki) / n_distinct(institutions_df_de_sector$ror) *100, 2), decimal.mark=".")`%). This could be attributed in particular to the fact that the COKI OA Dashboard, while covering a relatively long publication period (2000--2024), also includes institutions from multiple sectors, as well as institutions with a relatively low publication volume -- typically at least 50 publications [@COKI_how;@COKI_data].

@fig-2 also shows that, of the `r format(sum(institutions_df_de_sector$sir), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions included in the SCImago Institutions Ranking, `r format(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_sector, sir == 1 & lr == 0 & lroe == 0 & qs == 0 & coki == 0)$sir), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions (`r format(round(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_sector, sir == 1 & lr == 0 & lroe == 0 & qs == 0 & coki == 0)$sir) / n_distinct(institutions_df_de_sector$ror) *100, 2), decimal.mark=".")`%) are not included in any other ranking. By contrast, all institutions from both versions of the Leiden Ranking and from the QS Sustainability Ranking are also featured in at least one other ranking. In total, there are only `r format(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_sector, coki == 1 & lr == 1 & lroe == 1 & qs == 1 & sir == 1)$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions (`r format(round(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_sector, coki == 1 & lr == 1 & lroe == 1 & qs == 1 & sir == 1)$coki) / n_distinct(institutions_df_de_sector$ror) *100, 2), decimal.mark=".")`%) included in all five ranking systems.

Whereas the QS Sustainability Ranking and both versions of the Leiden Ranking include only higher education institutions in their rankings, the COKI OA Dashboard and the SCImago Institutions Ranking also cover institutions from other sectors. Higher education institutions are classified as *Education* in the COKI dataset, whilst in the SCImago Institutions Ranking dataset, the *Universities* sector is assigned to higher education institutions. In order to subsequently examine the institutional overlap of German higher education institutions across the five ranking systems, a *sector* column was added to the consolidated dataset of all ranking systems. For institutions featured in both versions of the Leiden Ranking or in the QS Sustainability Ranking, the sector classification *Universities* was added. For institutions featured in the SCImago Institutions Ranking or the COKI OA Dashboard, the original classification was retained. The dataset was then filtered to include only those institutions to which the values *Universities* or *Education* had been assigned in the *sector* column.

@fig-3 below shows the institutional overlap between the rankings with regard to German universities. The figure also includes only those institutions to which ROR IDs could be assigned.

![Institutional overlap for German universities with ROR IDs across five ranking systems](plots/univs_de_institution_upset.png){#fig-3 group="upset"}

In total, `r format(n_distinct(institutions_df_de_univs$ror), big.mark = ".")` different German higher education institutions were identified across all ranking systems. @fig-3 shows that the COKI OA Dashboard also covers significantly more German higher education institutions than any other ranking system, both in total (`r format(sum(institutions_df_de_univs$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions, `r format(round(sum(institutions_df_de_univs$coki) / n_distinct(institutions_df_de_univs$ror) *100, 2), decimal.mark=".")`%), as well as in terms of the number of institutions not included in any other ranking system (`r format(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_univs, coki == 1 & lr == 0 & lroe == 0 & qs == 0 & sir == 0)$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions, `r format(round(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_univs, coki == 1 & lr == 0 & lroe == 0 & qs == 0 & sir == 0)$coki) / n_distinct(institutions_df_de_univs$ror) *100, 2), decimal.mark=".")`%). According to the Federal Statistical Office, a total of 422 German higher education institutions were recorded in the 2024/2025 winter term [@destatis]. Thus, the COKI OA Dashboard currently represents `r format(round(n_distinct(institutions_df_de_univs$ror) / 422 * 100,2), decimal.mark=".")`% of all German higher education institutions. It is also the only ranking system that includes higher education institutions not featured in any other ranking. The total number of German higher education institutions featured in all five ranking systems, with `r format(sum(filter(institutions_df_de_univs, coki == 1 & lr == 1 & lroe == 1 & qs == 1 & sir == 1)$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` institutions, remains unchanged from the total number of all German institutions featured in all five ranking systems.

The COKI OA Dashboard and the SCImago Institutions Ranking are the only two of the ranking systems examined that do not limit their rankings to higher education institutions. With regard to Germany, of the total `r format(sum(institutions_df_de_sector$coki), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` German institutions featured in the COKI OA Dashboard, `r format(round(sum(institutions_df_de_univs$coki) / sum(institutions_df_de_sector$coki) *100,2), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")`% are German higher education institutions. By comparison, of the total `r format(sum(institutions_df_de_sector$sir), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")` German institutions featured in the SCImago Institutions Ranking, `r format(round(sum(institutions_df_de_univs$sir) / sum(institutions_df_de_sector$sir) *100,2), big.mark=",", decimal.mark=".")`% are German higher education institutions. For both ranking systems, it can therefore be observed that the majority of the German institutions included are assigned to other sectors.

Although all five rankings have a global focus, the figures are intended to visualise whether there are differences in geographical distribution between the rankings. To ensure better comparability, the analysis has been restricted to those institutions classified under the higher education sector (*Universities*, *Education*).

Looking at the absolute numbers of higher education institutions, Figures -@fig-leidenmaps and -@fig-maps show in particular that, for both versions of the Leiden Ranking and the SCImago Institutions Ranking, the majority of higher education institutions are based in China (LR: `r pref_df$nij_lr[pref_df$country == "China"]` institutions, LROE: `r pref_df$nij_lroe[pref_df$country == "China"]` institutions, SIR: `r pref_df$nij_sir[pref_df$country == "China"]` institutions). By contrast, for the QS Sustainability Ranking and the COKI OA Dashboard, most institutions are based in the United States of America (QS: `r pref_df$nij_qs[pref_df$country == "United States"]` institutions, COKI: `r pref_df$nij_coki[pref_df$country == "United States"]` institutions). Furthermore, the figures illustrate that, with the exception of the COKI OA Dashboard, certain countries, particularly those in the Global South, are not represented at all in the ranking systems.

In addition to the absolute number of higher education institutions per country and ranking system, below we examine the over- or under-representation of countries within the ranking systems using the *preference* as defined by @Moed2016. @Moed2016 defines *preference* as[^6]:

> The preference of ranking system R for a particular country C is expressed as the ratio of the actual and the expected number of institutions from C appearing in R, where the expected number is based on the total number of institutions across countries and across systems, under the assumption of independence of these two variables. A value of 1.0 indicates that the number of institutions from C in R is ‘as expected’.


The resulting *preference score* therefore measures whether a country, in terms of the number of institutions based there, is over- or under-represented within a ranking system. A value of 1 is neutral, i.e. the number of institutions from a country in a ranking system corresponds to expectations. Values above 1 indicate that more institutions from a country are included in a ranking system than expected. Values below 1 indicate that fewer institutions from a country are included in a ranking system than expected.


@tbl-pref shows, for all five ranking systems, the top five countries as measured by *preference score*. It displays the absolute number of higher education institutions and the respective *preference score* for each country, and additionally includes the values for Germany.

@tbl-pref reveals considerable differences in the geographical over-representation of the ranking systems. The traditional Leiden Ranking features a diverse range of countries without a consistent regional pattern (Luxembourg, Malta, China, Australia, Spain). The Leiden Ranking Open Edition features a greater number of countries from the Global South, as well as a few other countries outside the established academic centres of North America and Western Europe (Grenada, Cameroon, South Africa, Turkey, Italy), whilst the QS Sustainability Ranking focuses predominantly on Asian countries and territories (Brunei, Hong Kong, Saudi Arabia, Fiji, Azerbaijan). The regional focus of the Leiden Ranking Open Edition suggests an effect resulting from the inclusion of so-called *non-core publications* as well as a lower publication threshold. This expansion specifically captures more universities from countries such as India, Indonesia and Brazil, which are under-represented in the traditional Leiden Ranking [@vanEck2025c]. In the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the COKI OA Dashboard, the top five countries each share an identical preference score (2.69 and 1.70 respectively). This is due to the fact that the respective countries are represented exclusively in their respective ranking systems. It is also striking that the top five countries in the SCImago Institutions Ranking are represented by just a single institution each.

With regard to Germany, @tbl-pref presents a mixed picture. Whilst the traditional Leiden Ranking (1.44), the QS Sustainability Ranking (1.14) and the Leiden Ranking Open Edition (1.02) show a slightly above-average representation of German universities, the COKI OA Dashboard (0.99) is close to the expected value and the SCImago Institutions Ranking (0.85) is even slightly below it. Germany is therefore not among the top five countries in any of the five systems.

[^6]: In mathematical terms, @Moed2016 defines the *preference* as: $P= \bigg(\dfrac{n[i, j]}{\sum_i n[i, j]}\bigg)\bigg(\dfrac{\sum_i\sum_jn[i, j]} {\sum_jn[i, j]}\bigg)$, where $n[i, j]$ is the number of institutions from country $i$ in ranking system $j$, $\sum_in[i, j]$ is the sum of all $n[i, j]$ over all $i$ (countries), $\sum_jn[i, j]$ denotes the sum of all $n[i, j]$ over all $j$ (ranking systems), and $\sum_i\sum_jn[i, j]$ denotes the sum of all $n[i, j]$ over all $i$ (countries) and all $j$ (ranking systems).


### Data Sources

This section examines the data sources used by the five rankings, focusing on the following two categories of data sources: 1) data sources used to obtain bibliographic data, and 2) data sources used to determine open access status. Differences in the coverage, completeness and methodology of these data sources can lead to discrepancies in the calculation of metrics and thus limit the comparability of results across different rankings. Furthermore, the study examines whether the data sources used result in disciplinary differences between the rankings.

#### Bibliographic Data Sources

@Huang2020b identify two key sources of information that are necessary for the analysis of research outputs. Firstly, information sources that provide data to link research outputs to the relevant units of analysis (e.g. universities, research institutions). Secondly, information sources that provide data to link research outputs to relevant metrics (e.g. open access status) [@Huang2020b]. In the context of compiling university rankings, bibliographic data sources play a central role in providing this data and are essential for a quantitative assessment of the respective productivity of the universities under consideration.

@tbl-1 below shows the bibliographic data sources used by the five ranking systems. 

| Ranking | Web of Science | Scopus | OpenAlex | Crossref |
|:---------|:---------------:|:--------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| Leiden Ranking |  x | | | |
| Leiden Ranking Open Edition | | | x | |
| SCImago Institutions Ranking | | x | | |
| QS Sustainability Ranking | | x | | |
| COKI OA Dashboard | | | | x |

: Data sources used for the collection of bibliographic data {#tbl-1}

As @tbl-1 shows, the five rankings examined use four different bibliographic data sources: Web of Science (WoS), Scopus, Crossref and OpenAlex. Of these, Web of Science (WoS) is the most established abstract and citation database [@Birkle2020]. Until the mid-2000s, WoS was the leading tool for bibliometric analyses [@Gauch2023]. In 2004, Elsevier launched Scopus, the first comparable multidisciplinary database, which broke WoS’s previous monopoly [@Baas2020;@Huang2020;@Gauch2023]. Crossref was established in 2000 as a membership-based DOI registration agency. Publishers and other publication infrastructures can register DOIs for their publications via Crossref and, at the same time, submit publication metadata to the service. Since 2013, Crossref has offered a REST API through which Crossref’s publication metadata is openly accessible and can be reused [@Hendricks2020]. In 2022, OpenAlex was introduced as an open data source, with the aim of succeeding the discontinued Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG) as a fully open source of research information [@Priem2022]. Since its launch, OpenAlex has established itself as a serious alternative to proprietary providers, particularly through the integration of data from diverse open data sources such as Crossref, PubMed, ORCID and institutional repositories [@Torres2026;@Abramo2026].

The emergence of new data sources usually leads to comparative analyses in order to understand the differences between them and to situate them within the evolving research and infrastructure landscape [@Gauch2023]. The study by @Torres2026 provides a recent overview of comparative analyses, however, these analyses focus predominantly on WoS, Scopus, Microsoft Academic/Microsoft Academic Graph and OpenAlex. By contrast, there are comparatively few bibliometric studies that explicitly include Crossref in comparisons with other data sources.

The study by @Harzing2019 compared the quantitative coverage of Crossref and Dimensions with that of Google Scholar, Microsoft Academic, Scopus and Web of Science in terms of publication output and citation rates for the author’s publications, as well as for six leading journals in the field of Business & Economics. @Harzing2019 found that Crossref and Dimensions had higher publication coverage than Scopus and WoS for journal articles, book chapters and conference papers, but lower publication coverage than Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic across all document types considered. @Harzing2019 also found that open data sources have an advantage over proprietary data sources in terms of timeliness, as they often capture publications within a few weeks of their online publication, whilst Scopus and WoS often only index publications upon their print publication. The study by @Harzing2019 concludes that Crossref and Dimensions represent alternatives to the established commercial data sources, whereas Google Scholar and Microsoft Academic are more comprehensive open data sources.

The study by @Visser2021 carried out a pair-wise comparison of Scopus with the bibliographic data sources WoS (in the version licensed by the Centre for Science and Technology Studies (CWTS), which includes the SCIE, SSCI, AHCI, CPCI indexes), Dimensions, Crossref and Microsoft Academic in terms of document coverage, as well as the completeness and accuracy of citation links. @Visser2021 identified Microsoft Academic as offering the broadest coverage of documents, followed by Dimensions/Crossref, Scopus and CWTS WoS. Microsoft Academic also includes a larger number of non-scholarly documents. By contrast, @Visser2021 reported that Scopus and WoS are superior to Dimensions and Microsoft Academic in terms of the completeness and accuracy of citation links. Furthermore, a structural problem was identified with Crossref, as some citation links are not openly accessible, even though they are available internally within Crossref. @Visser2021 conclude that the choice of a suitable data source must be guided by the objectives of the analysis, and that both the comprehensiveness of Dimensions and Microsoft Academic and the selectivity of Scopus and WoS can offer added value.

@Kramer2022 analysed the coverage of funding information for NWO-funded publications in Crossref, The Lens, Web of Science, Scopus and Dimensions. The analysis revealed that Crossref provided funding information for only 67% of publications, with NWO being correctly identified by its funder ID in just 45% of cases. In contrast, Web of Science (83%) and Scopus (78%) achieved a significantly higher level of completeness in funding information, as they extracted this from the full texts, whilst Crossref relied exclusively on metadata submitted by publishers.

The study by @Asubiaro2023 compared the coverage of African journals in Web of Science, Scopus and Crossref. @Asubiaro2023 found that African journals were covered to a significantly greater extent in Crossref than in Web of Science and Scopus. Overall, however, @Asubiaro2023 assess African research as being under-represented in global citation databases.

The study by @Torres2026 combined a systematic literature review with an empirical bibliometric analysis to compare Web of Science, Scopus and OpenAlex. The literature review by @Torres2026 analysed five key areas: total volume of records, coverage of open access journals, language coverage, reference coverage, and the quality and reliability of metadata. The empirical section compared the three data sources, particularly with regard to document types, languages and research fields for publications between 2015 and 2024. @Torres2026 report that WoS and Scopus operate subscription-based business models with strictly curated, predominantly English-language content and exhibit a high degree of structural overlap between them. OpenAlex, by contrast, offers an open-source platform with heterogeneous data sources and exhibits a higher volume of records, greater linguistic and geographical diversity – particularly with regard to open access publications and publications from the Global South – as well as less overlap with the proprietary systems. With regard to metadata quality, @Torres2026 found that OpenAlex exhibits higher error rates in the identification and classification of document types, publication years, language and affiliation information than WoS and Scopus. In terms of subject areas, @Torres2026 report that WoS and Scopus have a similarly strong focus on the natural sciences, whereas OpenAlex indexes a significantly higher proportion of publications from the social sciences and humanities. Furthermore, @Torres2026 found that WoS and Scopus offer greater coverage and accuracy of references, whilst OpenAlex under-represents a considerable proportion of resources, particularly grey literature. @Torres2026 conclude that no single data source provides a comprehensive picture of the global scientific landscape and that the combined use of all three data sources can reduce disciplinary, linguistic and geographical biases.

The study by @Abramo2026 compared Web of Science, Scopus, and OpenAlex—both at the individual level and at the aggregated institutional level—in terms of publication output, impact metrics, and the resulting rankings. For Italian professors and universities in the field of management engineering, the comparison showed that the consistency among the data sources was high for pure publication output but only moderate for impact-based metrics. At the institutional level, the rankings of individual universities shifted—in some cases substantially—depending on the data source used, with smaller institutions being particularly affected. @Abramo2026 identified differences in disciplinary taxonomies, normalization procedures, and conventions for determining publication years as the main causes. These factors had a particular impact on rankings, especially when aggregating data at the institutional level. @Abramo2026 therefore recommend triangulating results from at least two data sources in evaluations, transparently reporting the sensitivity of the results, and—when using OpenAlex—explicitly defining and communicating methodological conventions in advance, including the definition of the document types to be included.

The study by @Huang2020 is already somewhat dated, but it is particularly interesting in the context of university rankings. @Huang2020 compared Web of Science, Scopus, and Microsoft Academic at the institutional level and examined their impact on university rankings. The results showed that the choice of data source led to clear differences in the bibliographic characteristics examined (document coverage, publication years, document types, citation rates, open access status, affiliation assignment). @Huang2020 found that Microsoft Academic offered the most comprehensive document coverage, particularly in the social sciences and humanities, but had less precise affiliation metadata. WoS and Scopus showed lower overall coverage but were more reliable in assigning institutions to publications. With regard to publication years, the sources showed a high degree of agreement overall, however, considerable discrepancies between the data sources occurred for individual institutions, notably those from non-English-speaking countries. @Huang2020 reported that the proportion of open access publications at the institutional level varied depending on the source, which also led to shifts in the rankings, with universities from non-English-speaking regions being disproportionately affected. With regard to document types, it was found that Microsoft Academic captured a higher proportion of book chapters and conference papers, while Scopus frequently indexed books and monographs that were not captured by the other sources. In terms of citation rates, the study showed that Microsoft Academic tended to report lower average values, which led to clear changes in ranking positions when the data source was switched. Universities that did not achieve top positions in international rankings were particularly affected. Overall, the study showed that relying on a single data source can cause distortions in the evaluation of universities, especially for non-Western institutions and those that rank lower in international rankings. The key recommendation from @Huang2020 was therefore to integrate multiple data sources for robust evaluation systems to enable a fair and comprehensive analysis.

The literature on the four bibliographic data sources examined -- Web of Science, Scopus, Crossref, and OpenAlex -- shows that all sources have advantages and disadvantages, each of which affects the evaluation of research performance and the production of university rankings.Web of Science and Scopus tend to be characterised by a high degree of structural reliability, precise affiliation assignments and more accurate citation tracking, however, they are limited by a selective content profile dominated by English-language material and by lower coverage of open access publications and research from the Global South. Crossref offers high timeliness and comprehensive coverage of publications, particularly for formats such as conference papers and book chapters, but suffers from incomplete funding information and structurally limited accessibility of citation links. OpenAlex positions itself as a comprehensive, open alternative with the largest volume of data, greater linguistic and geographical diversity, and stronger representation of research outputs from the social sciences and humanities. At the same time, OpenAlex tends to exhibit lower metadata quality, particularly in terms of document type classification, language detection and reference coverage. In addition, the studies by @Huang2020, @Torres2026 and @Abramo2026 demonstrate that the choice of data source not only influences quantitative coverage but is also decisive for the rankings of higher education institutions, specifically those from non-English-speaking regions. The results suggest that no single data source can provide a complete and fair representation of the global research landscape. Rather, the literature considers the combined use of multiple sources to be necessary in order to reduce disciplinary, linguistic and geographical biases and to create robust, transparent and fairer evaluation systems. It should also be noted, however, that the respective studies can only ever provide a snapshot of the data sources under investigation.

#### Open Access Data Sources

Determining the open access status of academic publications is a prerequisite for calculating open access indicators. This section provides an overview of the data sources used by the rankings examined to determine the open access status of the respective publications, as well as their specific characteristics. To this end, @tbl-2 first sets out below the open access data sources used by the five ranking systems examined.

| Ranking | Unpaywall | OpenAlex |
|:--------|:---------:|:--------:|
| Leiden Ranking | | x |
| Leiden Ranking Open Edition | | x | 
| SCImago Institutions Ranking | x | |
| QS Sustainability Ranking | x | |
| COKI OA Dashboard | x | |

: Data sources used to determine open access status {#tbl-2}


@tbl-2 shows that a total of two different open access data sources are used: Unpaywall and OpenAlex. The SCImago Institutions Ranking, the QS Sustainability Ranking and the COKI OA Dashboard all use Unpaywall, whereas both versions of the Leiden Ranking rely on OpenAlex to determine open access status.

Unpaywall is a free, automated service that identifies open access versions of articles using DOIs. The foundations for Unpaywall were laid as early as 2011; part of the underlying technology was published in 2016, and the Unpaywall browser plug-in was released in 2017 [@Else2018]. The service exclusively records publications with Crossref DOIs and is primarily focused on journal articles and preprints [@unpaywall_faq; @unpaywall_dois]. Other document types with Crossref DOIs, such as book chapters or conference papers, are in principle also processed by Unpaywall, as the *genre* field in the Unpaywall data schema directly adopts the Crossref type [@unpaywall_dataformat]. However, Unpaywall itself makes no statements regarding the quality of coverage for these document types [@unpaywall_faq]. In addition to publications without a Crossref DOI, so-called component DOIs are structurally not covered [@unpaywall_improvements2025] -- Crossref assigns these to individual components of journal articles, such as figures, tables or supplementary materials [@crossref_components]. The OA status determination is based on several open data sources, including Crossref, DOAJ and PubMed Central. Furthermore, Unpaywall harvests over 50,000 online sources, including journals, as well as institutional and subject-specific repositories [@unpaywall_sources]. Specifically, Unpaywall harvests repositories via the OAI-PMH protocol and cross-checks the metadata obtained in this way against the DOIs in its database. In addition, publishers’ landing pages are scraped directly to extract licence information not stored in Crossref. Furthermore, Unpaywall carries out manual corrections for known issues or misclassifications [@oadoi_github]. Only sources that make full texts accessible without the need to register and without CAPTCHA prompts are counted as OA sources [@unpaywall_locations]. Based on this information, Unpaywall assigns an OA status to each publication, distinguishing between five categories [@unpaywall_dataformat]: Gold, Hybrid, Green, Bronze and Closed. This classification logic follows a fixed decision-making sequence [@unpaywall_oa_status; @oadoi_github], which is schematically illustrated in @fig-mermaid.

:::{#fig-mermaid .column-page}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10

flowchart LR

    B -->|FALSE| D(closed)
    B -->|TRUE| C{best OA location?}
    C -->|repository| E(green)
    C -->|publisher| F{fully OA journal?} --- G
    F -->|TRUE| H(gold) 
    H --> L{APC = 0?}
    subgraph OpenAlex [" "]
    L -->|TRUE| M(diamond)
    OAlabel(OpenAlex) ~~~ M
    end
    L -->|FALSE| H
    F -->|FALSE| I{open license?}
    I --->|TRUE| J(hybrid)
    I -->|FALSE| K(bronze)

style D fill:#D6D3D1,stroke:#A6A09B,color:#000 
style E fill:#50C878,stroke:#059669,color:#fff
style H fill:#f59e0b,stroke:#d97706,color:#fff
style J fill:#C3B1E1,stroke:#8C68C4,color:#fff
style K fill:#CD7F32,stroke:#B87333,color:#fff
style M fill:#6495ED,stroke:#0047AB,color:#fff
style OpenAlex fill:#D3D3D3,color:#000 
style OAlabel fill:none,stroke:none,color:#000
G@{ shape: braces, label: "journal_is_in_doaj = true  

OR

journal_is_in_doaj = false & fully OA-publisher

OR

jorunal_is_in_doaj = false & only OA-articles" }
```

Determining open access status in Unpaywall (OpenAlex)
:::

First, the system checks whether an article is available via open access. It then checks whether the best available version is hosted by the publisher or in a repository; if it is hosted by the publisher, the journal’s OA status and the presence of an open licence determine whether it is classified as Gold, Hybrid or Bronze. A decisive factor for the classification as Gold is whether a journal is considered to be fully open access, which Unpaywall determines on the basis of three criteria [@unpaywall_gold_journal]: Erstens gilt eine Zeitschrift als Gold-OA, wenn sie im DOAJ gelistet ist. However, as the DOAJ does not cover all Gold OA journals, secondly, journals from well-known OA publishers are classified as Gold OA via a maintained whitelist; and thirdly, Unpaywall empirically assesses whether a journal publishes exclusively OA articles. If several OA versions of an article are available, Unpaywall uses a scoring algorithm to select the best OA source, with publisher versions ranked higher than repository versions, peer-reviewed versions ranked higher than preprints, and versions with a direct PDF link ranked higher than versions without [@unpaywall_best_location; @oadoi_github]. The OA status is then derived deterministically from the best OA source selected. In May 2025, Unpaywall’s underlying codebase was revised to improve speed, maintainability and data quality, and to enable community-led correction of errors [@unpaywall_update2025]. As part of this overhaul, Gold OA detection was also specifically expanded, including through the evaluation of data from OJS journals, J-STAGE and SciELO, in order to improve coverage beyond the DOAJ [@unpaywall_improvements2025].

OpenAlex has already been introduced in the previous section as a bibliographic data source. As such, unlike Unpaywall, OpenAlex does not limit itself to publications with a Crossref DOI when indexing research information. Prior to the OpenAlex-Walden rewrite in November 2025, OpenAlex and Unpaywall were operated by the same organisation on separate code bases, which occasionally led to discrepancies between the OA status information provided by the two services in the context of OA status determination [@openalex_rewrite;@unpaywall_improvements2025]. However, the OA status determination in OpenAlex followed a logic analogous to that of Unpaywall (see @fig-mermaid) with the same five categories: Gold, Hybrid, Bronze, Green and Closed -- the Diamond category was not implemented as a separate category until July 2024. Following the OpenAlex-Walden rewrite in November 2025, both systems are now operated on the same codebase, and Unpaywall has since been running as a subroutine of the OpenAlex infrastructure [@priem2025openalex;@openalex_2025review]. The Walden source code shows that this specifically means that OpenAlex work data indexed in Crossref is extracted and converted into the Unpaywall format [@openalex_createwunpaywall_2025], which should structurally rule out any discrepancies between the two services. The Walden pipeline determines the OA status in two stages [@openalex2025createworksbase]: First, at source level, a check is carried out to determine whether a journal is fully OA (via DOAJ, J-STAGE or observed OA rate). Building on this, each publication is assigned a status -- Diamond, Gold, Hybrid, Bronze, Green or Closed -- depending on accessibility, APC costs, licence and hosting location, with the best OA version being prioritised according to version type and PDF availability, in line with Unpaywall [@openalex2025createworksbase]. Since July 2024, OpenAlex has been assigning the *Diamond* OA status category, which identifies publications in purely open access journals without APCs. @haupka2026walden demonstrated empirically that the Walden rewrite has led to noticeable shifts in the OA classification. Diamond OA was awarded much more frequently following the rewrite, while Gold, Bronze and Hybrid OA declined. These findings highlight that individual releases on OpenAlex can have an impact on OA indicators and, at the same time, illustrate that OpenAlex is evolving dynamically [@haupka2026walden].

For rankings that use OpenAlex as their OA data source, this means that OA metrics depend not only on the underlying classification logic but also on the snapshot of data used -- a limitation that must be taken into account when interpreting the results of the Leiden Ranking and the Leiden Ranking Open Edition. For rankings that use Unpaywall as a data source, the introduction of the Diamond category has no immediate impact: in the Unpaywall export, Diamond is mapped to Gold [@openalex_createwunpaywall_2025], as the Unpaywall data schema does not provide for Diamond as a separate OA status value [@unpaywall_dataformat]. The SCImago Institutions Ranking, the QS Sustainability Ranking and the COKI OA Dashboard therefore classify Diamond articles as Gold and are structurally unable to report the Diamond category until the Unpaywall schema is expanded accordingly. Rankings that use OpenAlex directly, on the other hand, have Diamond available as a separate category and could potentially include it in their OA indicators in the future.


#### Document Types

@tbl-doctype below provides an overview of the document types covered by each ranking. It should be noted that the rankings use different type vocabularies -- Crossref types for COKI, Scopus types for the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking, OpenAlex types for the Leiden Ranking Open Edition, and WoS types for the traditional Leiden Ranking -- meaning that nominally identical terms such as *article* do not necessarily describe the same content [@Alperin2024;@Haupka2026].

| Ranking                      | Document types                |
|:-----------------------------|:------------------------------|
| Leiden Ranking               | article, review               |
| Leiden Ranking Open Edition  | article, review, book chapter | 
| SCImago Institutions Ranking | article, book, book chapter, conference paper, data paper, editorial, letter, note, review, short survey |
| QS Sustainability Ranking    | article, article in press, review, conference paper, book, book chapter, business article, data paper, report |
| COKI OA Dashboard            | journal articles, proceedings articles, reports, posted content, edited books, books, book chapters, book parts, book sections, reference books, monographs, reference entries, other |

: Document types covered {#tbl-doctype}

The five rankings differ noticeably in terms of the types of documents they cover. The traditional Leiden Ranking is limited to articles and reviews in international journals [@LR_indicators]. The Leiden Ranking Open Edition additionally includes book chapters in journals and book series [@LROE_indicators]. The QS Sustainability Ranking takes into account not only articles and reviews but also conference papers, books, book chapters, articles in press, business articles, data papers and reports, however, it excludes editorials, letters, notes and short surveys [@QS_paperdef]. The SCImago Institutions Ranking is the most inclusive of the Scopus-based rankings and takes into account all Scopus document types with the exception of the types retracted, erratum and preprint -- including editorials, letters and notes, which QS explicitly excludes [@SIR_method]. The COKI OA Dashboard is the most inclusive overall and includes almost all Crossref document types, including monographs, book chapters, conference papers, reports and posted content -- the only exclusions are datasets, databases, peer reviews, conference proceedings and a few other less traditional document types [@COKI_how].

These differences are particularly relevant for the calculation of OA indicators, as the proportion of OA publications can vary depending on the document type. Furthermore, publications without a Crossref DOI are not structurally covered by Unpaywall [@unpaywall_dois]. Consequently, the reported OA proportion for rankings that use Unpaywall as their OA data source may not provide a complete picture of the OA landscape, despite broad coverage of document types. Furthermore, differences regarding the document types included can have disciplinary implications, which are examined in more detail in the following section. The inclusion of different document types could therefore systematically result in different OA percentages even for identical institutions and publication periods, which would limit the comparability of the ranking results.


#### Disciplinary Differences

> A concern in any university evaluation is the existing disciplinary bias in large bibliographic sources used to support rankings. [@Huang2020a]

Disciplinary differences or biases that arise from the choice of bibliographic data sources when compiling a ranking may adversely affect the comparability of results across ranking systems by under- or over-representing different disciplines. This section examines the extent of disciplinary differences with regard to the open access dimension. However, as only the datasets from the two versions of the Leiden Ranking include disciplinary classification, the analysis is limited to the disciplinary differences between the traditional Leiden Ranking, which uses Web of Science as its bibliographic data source, and the Leiden Ranking Open Edition, which uses OpenAlex as its bibliographic data source.

To enable users to compare the results between the two versions of the Leiden Ranking, the CWTS has been providing interactive dashboards since the 2023 edition [@LROE_resources]. The results can be filtered by time period, one or more countries, fields and all indicators included in the Leiden Rankings, enabling a detailed comparison. @fig-fields incorporates the interactive dashboard for the 2025 edition of the Leiden Rankings. The x-axis represents the traditional Leiden Ranking, while the y-axis represents the Leiden Ranking Open Edition.
