The median absolute rank shift for Germany ranges from 2 positions in the *Life and earth sciences* field to 8 positions in the *Physical sciences and engineering* field. The 90th percentile ranges from 8.3 (*All sciences*) to 21.4 positions (*Physical sciences and engineering*). In the field *Physical sciences and engineering*, German institutions therefore show greater variation -- both in typical cases and at the upper end of the distribution -- than in other fields. The field *Life and earth sciences* exhibits the lowest median value among the six fields, at 2, while the 90th percentile, at 8.8, is close to the median and well below the corresponding value for *Physical sciences and engineering*. This suggests a comparatively even distribution, one that is not heavily influenced by individual institutions with high volatility. In the field of *Mathematics and computer science*, German institutions typically fluctuate by 6 positions and, in one tenth of cases, by 16.6 positions. The example for *Mathematics and computer science* shown in @tbl-lrshift (rank shifts of between one and five positions for the top five institutions) lies at the lower end of the distribution observed for this field.

Globally, the median ranges between 39 and 59, and the 90th percentile between 124.5 and 199.3 positions. The field *Biomedical and health sciences* (median 59, 90th percentile 199.3) has the highest values for both the median and the 90th percentile amongst the six fields, while *All sciences* (median 39, 90th percentile 124.5) has the lowest. Consequently, the field most affected by changes in ranking at global level (*Biomedical and health sciences*) differs from the fields most affected in Germany (*Physical sciences and engineering*, *Mathematics and computer science*).

One possible explanation for the comparatively significant shifts in rankings in *Mathematics and computer science* and *Physical sciences and engineering* for German institutions lies in the methodological definition of *core publications* in both versions of the Leiden Ranking. The methodology of the traditional Leiden Ranking defines *core publications* for WoS exclusively as the document types *article* and *review*. By contrast, the definition used for OpenAlex is less restrictive [@vanEck2025b]. The reason for this is that, compared with proprietary databases, OpenAlex uses a significantly less granular document-type classification. Whereas WoS lists conference papers as a separate document type, clearly distinguished from *article/review*, OpenAlex groups journal articles, conference papers and preprints into a single *article* type as part of its document type classification; in OpenAlex, *article* effectively functions as a catch-all category [@Haupka2026;@Alperin2024]. This lower level of granularity has direct consequences for the *core-publications* count. Conference papers, which are excluded in WoS via explicit type assignment, are implicitly assigned to the generic *article* type in OpenAlex. Depending on the field and publication culture, this could result in differing counts, and fields characterised by the high significance of conference papers as a publication format might thus exhibit greater disciplinary differences. This also suggests that even standardised, size-independent indicators such as PP(OA) are not independent of data sources. This must be taken into account when comparing different ranking versions and interpreting their results.

It should be noted, however, that OpenAlex has since revised its own document type classification [@openalex_classification]. OpenAlex now categorises 25 different document types and, according to its own statements, the document type of around 10% of the indexed works have changed [@openalex_classification]. This will have a particular impact on future versions of the rankings that use OpenAlex as a data source.


### Open Access Indicators

Within evaluative bibliometrics, so-called productivity indicators focus on counting publication volumes in order to quantify the productivity of individuals, institutions or countries [@Gauch2023]. In this context, open access indicators can be understood as a form of productivity indicator, as they usually count the number of open access publications and use this to generate an approximate measure of the productivity of researchers, institutions or countries in the area of open access.

In line with good bibliometric practice, as outlined, for example, in the Leiden Manifesto [@Hicks2015], the selection of indicators used in the context of rankings requires careful consideration of their suitability for comparing institutions. A comparison between institutions from different regional contexts or with varying numbers of researchers and publication volumes can be problematic if the indicators merely represent absolute numbers of publications, as the specific conditions and challenges of each institution are not taken into account. To improve comparability between institutions, various forms of normalisation are therefore applied when constructing indicators [@Gauch2023]. One form of normalisation with regard to open access indicators could be to set the absolute number of an institution’s open access publications in relation to the absolute number of all its publications during the period under review.

In addition to individual indicators, so-called *composite indicators* are also used for certain rankings that are structured as league tables. These indicators are derived from weighted aggregates of individual indicators [@Glaenzel2009;@Johnes2018]. The idea behind composite indicators is to capture complex phenomena relating to scientific activities by combining and consolidating various indicators into a single, comprehensive metric. These linearised metrics, which can be ranked, make it easier to compare institutions, individuals or countries [@quick_notes]. Nevertheless, certain problems are associated with composite indicators -- a good overview can be found in @Forthmann2024. Among the problems and points of criticism are, for example, the fact that the selection of weightings for individual components in composite indicators is often opaque and, in some cases, arbitrary. Yet the weights of the individual components have a huge impact on the resulting ranking [@Glaenzel2009;@Forthmann2024]. Furthermore, criticism has been raised that there is often a lack of sufficient transparency regarding the construction of these indicators, which can make it difficult to interpret the ranking results [@Forthmann2024].

@tbl-oaindicators provides a summary of the key differences between the five ranking systems in terms of the open access indicators they use.

::: {#tbl-oaindicators}

| Ranking                      | OA data source | OA status types distinguished                     | Presentation form  | Weighting in overall score |
|:-----------------------------|:---------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:------------------|:---------------------------|
| Leiden Ranking               | OpenAlex       | Gold, Hybrid, Bronze, Green, Unknown              | Individual indicators (absolute & relative) | no overall score |
| Leiden Ranking Open Edition  | OpenAlex       | Gold, Hybrid, Bronze, Green                       | Individual indicators (absolute & relative) | no overall score |
| SCImago Institutions Ranking | Unpaywall      | no differentiation                                | single indicator (%) | 2% (within Research: 50%) |
| QS Sustainability Ranking    | Unpaywall      | Gold, Hybrid, Green                               | aggregated indicator (0–100) | 1% (within Governance: 10%) |
| COKI OA Dashboard            | Unpaywall      | Publisher Open, Other Platform Open, Both, Closed | absolute & relative | no overall score |

: Comparison of the open access indicators across the five ranking systems

:::

Both versions of the Leiden Ranking essentially provide two types of open access indicators: 1) indicators that show the total volume of open access publications produced by a higher education institution over a four-year period, and 2) indicators that show the proportion of open access publications out of the total publication volume of a higher education institution over a four-year period. Both indicators are reported once as a total for open access publications and, in addition, separately for the common open access status types (gold, hybrid, green, bronze, and unknown as used in the traditional Leiden Ranking). In addition to the open access indicators, the total publication volume per institution is also stated. Although a comparison between institutions based on absolute numbers has its limitations, it can still be useful to report absolute figures in order to improve the transparency and traceability of the indicators. Stating the absolute numbers enables institutions to verify the percentage figures and assess their accuracy.

Similar to the two Leiden Rankings, the COKI OA Dashboard also reports both absolute figures and relative proportions in relation to an institution’s open access publication volume. The scope of the indicators shown in the COKI OA Dashboard varies between the institutional overview page and the detailed pages for individual institutions. The overview page, which is designed to enable a comparison of all institutions represented in the COKI OA Dashboard, displays the following indicators for the publication period 2000–2024: 1) the percentage of open access publications, 2) a stacked bar chart showing the percentages of articles that are available via the publisher, other platforms, both, or not at all via open access. However, the bar chart does not show the respective percentages; 3) the total number of publications by an institution; and 4) the total number of open access publications by an institution. The detail pages for individual institutions contain further specific indicators that provide a more detailed overview of an institution’s open access publishing activity. Among other things, these pages display percentage figures for the stacked bar chart and trends over time. It is striking that there is a discrepancy between an institution’s overview page and its details page regarding the absolute figures for total publication volume and open access publication volume. The overview page shows the exact figures, whereas the details page displays rounded figures. Furthermore, the percentage of open access publications shown on both pages is a rounded figure. Although the use of absolute figures, similar to the Leiden Rankings, ensures greater verifiability of the indicators, the presentation of rounded figures is less precise.

The SCImago Institutions Ranking uses a composite indicator that aggregates various indicators from the three areas of *Research*, *Innovation* and *Societal*. The *Research* dimension accounts for 50% of the composite indicator and is therefore clearly more heavily weighted than the other two dimensions, which are weighted at 30% (*Innovation*) and 20% (*Societal*). In the SCImago Institutions Ranking, the open access indicator forms part of the *Research* dimension and is weighted at 2%. It is therefore one of the least heavily weighted indicators within the *Research* dimension and the composite indicator as a whole. The open access indicator represents the percentage of publications that are published in open access journals or indexed in Unpaywall [@SIR_method]. However, the SCImago Institutions Ranking does not report either the open access indicator or the total score achieved by the institutions, it merely states the resulting rank.

Similar to the SCImago Institutions Ranking, the QS Sustainability Ranking also uses a composite indicator. To this end, the QS Sustainability Ranking aggregates various indicators from the areas of *Environmental Impact*, *Social Impact* and *Governance*. The *Governance* dimension accounts for 10% of the composite indicator and is therefore given less weight than the other two dimensions, each of which is weighted at 45%. The open access indicator forms part of the *Governance* dimension in the QS Sustainability Ranking and accounts for 1% of this dimension. All indicators within the *Governance* dimension are assigned the same weighting and are therefore given equal consideration for the dimension. The open access indicator specifies the proportion of an institution’s total research output that is available in open access according to Unpaywall [@QS_governance]. In constructing the indicator, a distinction is made between different types of open access status (gold, hybrid, green) and subject areas, to which different weightings are assigned. The final open access indicator is aggregated based on the individual values per field and scaled to a range between 0 and 100 [@QS_governance]. In addition to the total score, the QS Sustainability Ranking dataset shows the score achieved for each dimension separately. The total score is only shown up to rank 902.

Overall, it is evident that the five ranking systems differ, in some cases considerably, in their use of open access indicators, even though all the open access indicators outlined measure and present the productivity of institutions in relation to open access.  Differences and challenges regarding the comparability of ranking results arise, for example, from the consideration of different types of open access status (gold, hybrid, green, etc.) for classifying open access publications. This also results in a path dependency on the data source used to identify open access publications. Both versions of the Leiden Ranking use OpenAlex as their data source for identifying open access publications and, furthermore, report the open access indicators separately for all open access status types. The QS Sustainability Ranking, on the other hand, uses Unpaywall as its data source, but appears to distinguish only between gold, hybrid and green open access publications [@QS_governance]. The SCImago Institutions Ranking also uses Unpaywall as its data source, but does not appear to distinguish between different types of open access status [@SIR_method]. The COKI OA Dashboard likewise uses Unpaywall as its data source for identifying open access publications, but, unlike the other rankings, does not display the typical open access status types with their corresponding colours. Instead, the COKI OA Dashboard groups gold, hybrid and bronze publications together under the category *Publisher Open*. These differences make it difficult to compare the ranking systems in terms of open access.

Due to the more nuanced presentation of the indicators, both versions of the Leiden Ranking and the COKI OA Dashboard require users to examine the individual dimensions separately in order to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the institutions. This entails a higher level of complexity when interpreting the results. The SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking simplify this complexity through the use of composite indicators. However, the composite indicators prove to be less suitable for open access monitoring and the assessment of open access activities, as the specific open access-related values cannot be derived directly from the composite indicators. Furthermore, open access indicators play a secondary role in the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking, as they each account for only a very small proportion of the overall score.


### Institutional Participation in Data Collection

This section examines the data collection methods used by the various ranking providers and explores the extent to which institutions can participate in the data collection process that concerns them.

For the traditional Leiden Ranking, the CWTS does not collect any data directly from the ranked institutions [@LR_method;@LR_general]. The ranking is based on data from the Web of Science, which is processed and standardised by the CWTS. However, as Web of Science is a proprietary data source subject to licensing restrictions, the CWTS is unable to make the raw data or the curated data openly accessible [@LeidenData]. Consequently, it is not readily possible for the institutions concerned to verify the quality of the data.

Similarly, no data is collected directly from the institutions for the Leiden Ranking Open Edition [@LROE_universities]. However, unlike the traditional Leiden Ranking, the Leiden Ranking Open Edition draws on open data sources, such as OpenAlex and ROR, to produce the ranking [@LROE_data]. Through the use of open data sources and thanks to the provision of raw and results data by the CWTS [@LROE_resources], the ranked institutions are able, on the one hand, to verify the quality of the data and, on the other hand, to participate in the data curation process by reporting any data quality issues to the relevant stakeholders [@LeidenData].

The methodology of the SCImago Institutions Ranking states that data for the ranking is collected from various sources, namely: Scopus, PATSTAT, Google, Semrush, Unpaywall, PlumX Metrics, Mendeley and Overton [@SIR_method]. The methodology makes no mention of any opportunity for institutional involvement in data collection, it is therefore assumed that no data is collected directly from the ranked institutions. The bibliographic data for the SCImago Institutions Ranking is retrieved from Scopus, a proprietary data source which, like Web of Science, is subject to licensing restrictions. The raw data for the SCImago Institutions Ranking is not publicly available, meaning that it can be assumed that ranked institutions do not readily have the opportunity to verify or correct the data relating to them before it is included in the ranking. To determine open access status, the SCImago Institutions Ranking uses Unpaywall, an open data source. As with the Leiden Ranking Open Edition, it may be possible for the institutions concerned to participate in the data curation process for the open access data by reporting data quality issues directly to Unpaywall. Overall, the methodology of the SCImago Institutions Ranking provides little information regarding data quality and possible limitations, nor is there any transparent communication regarding the options available to institutions for helping to improve data quality.

The COKI Open Access Dashboard exclusively uses open data sources for data collection, including Crossref, Unpaywall and ROR [@COKI_how]. The methodology of the COKI OA Dashboard describes the process of data collection from external data sources in detail, but provides no information regarding data provision by the ranked institutions themselves [@COKI_how]. It can therefore be assumed that there is no direct institutional involvement in the data collection process. As the COKI dataset is based on open data sources, it can further be assumed -- as with the Leiden Ranking Open Edition -- that the institutions concerned have the opportunity to participate indirectly in the data curation process by reporting data quality issues directly to the relevant data providers. Additionally, COKI communicates the limitations of its own dataset [@COKI_how] and provides various contact options [@COKI_contact], so that institutions also have the opportunity to play an active role in contributing to the improvement of the data in the COKI dataset.

The QS Sustainability Ranking is the only one of the five ranking systems examined that directly involves the institutions concerned in the data collection process. The methodology of the QS Sustainability Ranking states that QS generally encourages all institutions to provide data for the QS rankings [@QS_sustain]. QS provides a dedicated platform for data submission, however, the methodology does not provide a precise list of the data requested [@QS_sustain]. Should institutions that are eligible for inclusion in the QS Sustainability Ranking fail to provide data, QS assesses these institutions on the basis of proprietary and publicly available data, or data previously provided by the institution in question. A complete opt-out from the ranking by institutions is therefore not provided for. QS justifies this by arguing that the inclusion of all qualifying institutions enhances the reliability of the rankings [@QS_optout]. However, QS does not provide any information on how many of the ranked institutions actually take up the opportunity to submit data.

Overall, it appears that institutions only have limited opportunities to participate in the data collection process carried out by ranking providers. The QS Sustainability Ranking is the only ranking system that collects data directly from the institutions concerned, although it is not entirely clear what specific data is requested from them. The other ranking systems rely exclusively on data from external sources that are not collected directly from the institutions. However, the use of open data sources, such as in the Leiden Ranking Open Edition or the COKI OA Dashboard, can offer institutions an opportunity to improve the quality of the data relating to them. High-quality source data and transparent methodologies for compiling rankings can also help to improve confidence in the reliability and validity of the ranking systems.


## Limitations

This analysis is subject to several methodological limitations, which must be taken into account when interpreting the results.

The analysis of institutional overlap between the five ranking systems was restricted to German institutions due to incomplete ROR-ID mappings for the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking. The reported overlap percentages cannot therefore be readily extrapolated to the global level.

The analysis of disciplinary differences is limited to the two versions of the Leiden Ranking, as only these include disciplinary classifications in their data. It is not possible, on this basis, to draw conclusions regarding disciplinary biases in the other three ranking systems. The analysis of changes in ranking between the traditional Leiden Ranking and the Leiden Ranking Open Edition relates exclusively to the subset of institutions that are common to both, as identified by ROR IDs. For Germany, 15 of the 73 institutions included in the Leiden Ranking Open Edition were not represented in the traditional Leiden Ranking and were therefore excluded from the analysis. Furthermore, the absolute median and percentile values between the German (N = 53–58) and global samples (N = 1,207–1,586) were not directly comparable due to the considerable differences in sample size. Corresponding comparisons were therefore limited to qualitative observations within the respective levels.

All observations reported in this analysis represent snapshots of the respective underlying data versions. The same applies to the literature used regarding the bibliographic data sources. The studies reflect the state of Web of Science, Scopus, Crossref and OpenAlex at the time each analysis was conducted, and, due to the dynamic evolution of these data sources, the study results cannot simply be extrapolated to the current state.

## Summary

A comparative analysis of the five ranking systems, focusing on the open access dimension, shows that, despite a common interest -- the measurement of open access activities at research institutions -- the OA indicators used are only comparable to a limited extent. The main reasons for this limited comparability lie, in particular, in the following areas:

1. In the choice of bibliographic data source (Web of Science, Scopus, OpenAlex, Crossref), which determines both the coverage of publications and their disciplinary and geographical distribution.
2. In the choice of OA data source (Unpaywall vs. OpenAlex), which defines the available OA status categories and their classification logic.
3. In the document types included, which define the denominator for all relative OA indicators.
4. In the construction of the indicators themselves, which ranges from differentiated individual indicators to highly aggregated composite indicators.
5. In empirically observable differences between the rankings themselves: the systems examined differ considerably in the number and overlap of the institutions included (in particular, the COKI OA Dashboard shows much broader coverage than the other four rankings) as well as in the geographical representation of individual countries (see @tbl-pref). Using the two versions of the Leiden Ranking as an example, it was also found that the ranking position of individual institutions can shift noticeably depending on the data source used, and that the extent of this shift varies between disciplines as well as between Germany and the global level.

Consequently, both a direct comparison of the ranking results of individual institutions across the five systems and a comparison of their respective open access activities across multiple ranking systems are of limited value. Neither the underlying publication volumes nor the calculated open access proportions relate to comparable populations. Furthermore, institutions not included in a particular ranking cannot, in principle, use it to assess their own standing, whereas institutions featured in multiple rankings cannot have their respective results directly compared.

This has specific implications for users who wish to utilise rankings for open access monitoring or strategic decision-making. Rankings based on open data sources -- in particular the Leiden Ranking Open Edition and the COKI OA Dashboard -- offer greater transparency and traceability, as well as the opportunity to report data quality issues to the relevant entities. This offers advantages over ranking systems that rely on proprietary data sources. However, transparency alone does not resolve the fundamental problem of comparability between ranking systems. Rankings using composite indicators, such as the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking, are generally less suitable for nuanced OA monitoring, as the OA indicators each account for only a very small proportion of the overall score and no disaggregated OA figures are reported.

## Data Availability {.appendix}

This study is based on secondary data from five institutional ranking systems and the Research Organisation Registry (ROR). The data used are described in detail in the accompanying data documentation [@doerner2026data]. The data from the CWTS Leiden Rankings (Traditional Edition and Open Edition), the COKI Open Access Dashboard and the ROR dataset are publicly available under open licences and are cited in the data documentation with versioned, persistent DOIs. These data are not published separately as part of the dataset underlying the analysis, as this offers no added value compared with the existing, versioned sources.

The data from the SCImago Institutions Ranking and the QS Sustainability Ranking are not published for the following reasons: (1) The terms of use for the data from the SCImago Institutions Ranking are not sufficiently specific to determine whether redistribution is permitted, and (2) access to the data from the QS Sustainability Ranking requires registration with the data provider, whose terms of use also do not contain explicit permission for redistribution.

To ensure reproducibility despite these limitations, a data release comprising a data documentation that describes in detail all data sources, matching and harmonisation procedures, as well as the components of the data publication, and the complete computational notebook (Quarto/R source code) used to carry out the analysis, together with a rendered HTML version of the notebook including all calculations, tables, UpSet plots and choropleth maps generated during execution, has been deposited on Zenodo under a CC0 licence: Dörner, S. (2026). *Dataset for: Open Access in Institutional Rankings* [Dataset]. Zenodo. <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23892205>

Direct links and access conditions for each of the five original ranking data sets, as well as for the ROR data set, including the respective DOIs, are provided in the data documentation.
